newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-HOGAN THE LEGEND REMEMBERED IN MEMORIAL SERVICE.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-HOGAN THE LEGEND REMEMBERED IN MEMORIAL SERVICE.

text.p: Golfing fans and the game's stars mourned Ben Hogan on Tuesday as the legendary shotmaker was buried in Texas, leaving behind one of sport's great tales of courage and determination.
About 1,000 mourners attended a public memorial service for Hogan in Fort Worth's University Christian Church.
Hogan died last Friday at the age of 84. He had suffered from bronchitis and Alzheimer's disease and underwent surgery for colon cancer two years ago.
A single-minded competitor, Hogan dominated the world of golf in the 1940s and early 1950s and is widely considered to be the game's most creative shotmaker ever.
He had 63 PGA Tour victories, the third most of all time, and won nine major titles -- two Masters, four U.S. Opens, one British Open and two PGA Championships.
But behind Hogan's statistics lay a more impressive story -- his triumphant return to the sport after a life-threatening car accident in 1949, when he was 36.

Hogan's public memorial service drew a who's who of golfing powers and legends in their own right to the church, less than two miles from Colonial Country Club, known as, "Hogan's Alley," for the five Colonial PGA tournaments he won there.

Among those who paid their final respects were PGA Commissioner Tim Finchem, former Hogan competitors, Byron Nelson, Sam Snead, former U.S. Open champion Ken Venturi and two-time Masters champion Ben Crenshaw.
"We've lost one of the really good ones," said Snead, 85, who joined with Nelson and Hogan to form golf's, "Big Three," in the 1940s and '50s.

The Hogan family listed 25 honorary pallbearers, including two sportswriters. But Nelson, who had know Hogan since age 13, was not listed. He sat at the back of the church with his wife, and slipped out as soon as the service was over.
"We had so many good memories," Nelson said as he left the church. "I've been thinking about all the good times and great tournaments we had together."
Hogan and Nelson grew up in golf together as caddies at Fort Worth's Glen Garden Country Club and often travelled by car together to professional tournaments.
He said he couldn't explain the apparent final snub by his longtime friend and competitor.
"Ben was very private person. He didn't like people who bothered him. I didn't even have his home phone number," Nelson said.
Venturi, now a television broadcaster, was befriended by Hogan as a young player and said he often would call Hogan when he was in town to broadcast the Colonial tournament.
"We would talk about a lot of things," Venturi said. "He was always very nice and so kind to me."
Finchem said he felt it was important to fly in from his Florida headquarters to represent the PGA Tour, which Hogan dominated like few others during his career.

Hogan won nine major championships, including the Masters, U.S. and British Open in 1953, less than four years after a near-fatal car crash. He was the only golfer ever to win three majors in a single season.
Hogan is considered by many golf experts as among the greatest golfers of all time along with Nelson, Jack Nicklaus and Bobby Jones.
"There will never be another like him," Finchem said. "He was one of the true greats of the game and I thought it was important to be here to salute him as the passing of an era."
Crenshaw's professional career began after Hogan's had already ended, but he said he was inspired by the stoic Texan's professionalism and dedication.

"All he really wanted to do was play golf and be left alone doing it," Crenshaw said. "He didn't care about endorsements or fame or honours or anything else. His mother told him he only had one name and he shouldn't disgrace it and he never did."
Crenshaw, a noted golf historian, said the passing of Hogan was another great loss for those who love golf's rich tradition.
"We lost so many good ones lately, but Mr. Hogan was unique. He was more dedicated to golf than anyone I ever knew."

After his retirement from professional golf, Hogan founded the Ben Hogan golf equipment company, which still bears his name, and designed one golf course, The Trophy Club, located near the Dallas/Fort Worth Airport.
In the last year illness forced Hogan to stop his daily trips to Shady Oaks Country Club, where he used to sit for hours in the members' dining room which overlooked the 18th green.
